b: A Mallorcan Franciscan professor who at fifty walked the length of California founding nine missions from San Diego to San Francisco, baptising six thousand, defending the Indians against the soldiers, and walking on an ulcerated leg the whole way. Also today: Oliver Plunkett, hanged at Tyburn in 1681.

Before 1969 the Visitation was kept today, after the Octave of the Baptist. Also today: Processus and Martinian, the jailers of Peter in the Mamertine prison, converted and martyred; and Otto of Bamberg, apostle of Pomerania.

'Didymus', the twin, who said 'Let us also go, that we may die with him', asked 'Lord, we know not whither thou goest', and refused to believe the Resurrection until he touched the wounds — then made the fullest confession in the Gospels: 'My Lord and my God.' Tradition takes him to India, where the Christians of Kerala still call themselves his.

Great-niece of Elizabeth of Hungary, married at twelve to the faithless King Denis, who raised his illegitimate children, rode between two armies to stop a war between her husband and her son, and died a Franciscan tertiary on another peace mission. Also today: Independence Day (United States).

A physician of Cremona who became a priest and founded the Barnabites, the first clerks regular of the Catholic Reformation, promoting the Forty Hours' devotion and the ringing of bells at three on Friday afternoons. He died at thirty-six.

An eleven-year-old farm girl of the Pontine marshes stabbed fourteen times by a neighbour, Alessandro Serenelli, when she refused him; she forgave him before dying. He repented in prison after a dream of her, and attended her canonisation in 1950 with her mother.

An English monk who made a seven-year pilgrimage to the Holy Land — the earliest English travel narrative, dictated to a nun — and was sent by Boniface, his kinsman, to be first bishop of Eichstätt. Also today: Palladius, first bishop sent to the Irish.

t: Bishop and martyr, apostle of Franconia
b: An Irish missionary bishop killed at Würzburg with two companions for telling Duke Gozbert that his marriage to his brother's widow was unlawful. His skull is carried through Würzburg on his feast. Also today: Aquila and Priscilla, the tentmakers who taught Apollos.

A hundred and twenty martyrs of China, from 1648 to 1930: eighty-seven Chinese and thirty-three missionaries. Zhao Rong was a soldier who escorted a bishop to his execution, was converted by his bearing, became a priest, and was tortured to death in Sichuan. Also today: the Martyrs of Gorkum.

A Roman widow who watched her seven sons executed one by one under Marcus Aurelius and then died herself, encouraging each to look up to heaven. Also today: Knud, king of Denmark, and Rufina and Secunda, virgin martyrs of Rome.

The founder of Western monasticism (see March 21). His Rule balances prayer, work and reading — ora et labora — with a moderation that let it outlast every other. 'Listen, my son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart.' Paul VI named him patron of Europe in 1964.

A Florentine knight who met his brother's murderer unarmed on Good Friday, spared him when he begged in the form of the cross, and saw the crucifix in San Miniato bow to him. He became a monk, founded Vallombrosa and fought simony. Also today: Veronica, who wiped the face of Christ.

Duke of Bavaria and last Ottonian emperor, who founded the bishopric of Bamberg, supported Cluny's reform, and, tradition says, lived in continence with his wife Cunegund; both are saints. He asked to be received as a monk at Verdun and was ordered by the abbot to keep ruling.

A Mohawk girl of the Hudson valley, scarred and half-blinded by smallpox at four, baptised by Jesuits at twenty and driven from her village, who walked two hundred miles to the mission at Kahnawake and died at twenty-four. 'The Lily of the Mohawks', first Native American saint. Also today: Camillus de Lellis.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: The 'Seraphic Doctor', minister general of the Franciscans who wrote the official life of Francis and The Journey of the Mind to God; a cardinal who was found washing dishes when the red hat arrived. He died during the Council of Lyon, where Thomas Aquinas had been travelling to meet him.

The mountain where Elias called down fire, later home of the hermits who became the Carmelites. The brown scapular given to Simon Stock is the devotion's sign; Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross and Thérèse of Lisieux are its children.

Sixteen Carmelite nuns guillotined in Paris ten days before the fall of Robespierre, singing the Veni Creator as they mounted the scaffold one by one, the prioress last. Poulenc's opera Dialogues of the Carmelites tells their story. Also today: Alexis, the man of God, and Leo IV.

A giant of a soldier, gambler and brawler with an incurable leg wound, converted at twenty-five, who founded the Ministers of the Sick to nurse the dying in hospitals and on battlefields — the red cross on their habit preceded the Red Cross by three centuries. (July 14 in the new calendar.)

Eldest sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, who persuaded Basil to give up his rhetorician's ambition for monastic life, and turned the family estate into a monastery. Gregory's On the Soul and the Resurrection records her deathbed conversation.

By tradition a disciple of Peter sent to Ravenna as its first bishop, exiled and beaten repeatedly, and finally martyred at Classe, where the sixth-century basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe shows him among lambs in a green paradise. Also today: Margaret of Antioch, who burst from the dragon.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: A Capuchin who spoke Hebrew well enough to preach in synagogues, led the imperial army against the Turks at Székesfehérvár armed only with a crucifix, and died on an embassy to Spain on his sixtieth birthday. His collected works fill fifteen volumes.

Freed of seven demons, she followed Jesus from Galilee, stood at the cross, and came to the tomb while it was still dark — the first to see him risen, sent to tell the apostles. Gregory the Great's identification of her with the sinful woman of Luke 7 shaped a thousand paintings but is not in the text. Pope Francis raised the day to a feast in 2016.

A noblewoman and mother of eight who after her husband's death received visions she dictated in Swedish — the Revelations, read all over Europe — founded the Bridgettines at Vadstena, went to Rome to demand the pope's return from Avignon, and died there after a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

A Lebanese Maronite monk who spent his last twenty-three years in a hermitage at Annaya, silent, eating once a day, and died on Christmas Eve after a stroke at Mass. Lights over his grave, an incorrupt body and a flood of cures made him Lebanon's saint for Christians and Muslims alike.

Son of Zebedee, brother of John, 'son of thunder', present at the Transfiguration and Gethsemani, the first apostle to be martyred — beheaded by Herod Agrippa in 44. Spain claims his body at Compostela, the goal of Europe's great pilgrim road, the Camino.

t: Parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: The grandparents of Jesus, unnamed in Scripture, known from the second-century Protoevangelium of James: an old, childless couple whose prayer was answered with Mary. Anne became the patroness of mothers, grandmothers and Brittany; Luther called on her when the lightning struck.

Physician to the emperor Maximian at Nicomedia, who treated the poor for nothing and was beheaded under Diocletian; his blood at Ravello liquefies on his feast. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, patron of doctors. Also today: the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus.

Nazarius and the boy Celsus, martyrs of Milan whose bodies Ambrose discovered in 395; Victor I, the African pope who fixed Easter on a Sunday; and Innocent I, who condemned Pelagius. Also today: Samson of Dol, apostle of Brittany.

The family of Bethany where Jesus was at home. Martha, 'busy about much serving', who confessed 'Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God' before her brother was raised; Mary, who chose the better part; Lazarus, four days dead. Pope Francis joined the three in one memorial in 2021.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: 'Golden-worded' bishop of Ravenna when it was the imperial capital, whose short, vivid sermons — he feared boring his congregation — survive by the hundred. He told Eutyches to submit to the pope, 'since blessed Peter lives and presides in his own see.' Also today: Abdon and Sennen, Persian martyrs.

A Basque courtier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball at Pamplona; reading the lives of Christ and the saints in convalescence, he hung up his sword at Montserrat, wrote the Spiritual Exercises in a cave at Manresa, studied at Paris at thirty-three, and founded the Society of Jesus. 'For the greater glory of God.'

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: A Neapolitan lawyer who lost a case through his own error and left the bar for the priesthood, founded the Redemptorists to preach to the abandoned peasants of the hills, and wrote the Moral Theology that made confession gentler. He composed Christmas carols still sung in Italy. Patron of confessors.

A Sardinian, first bishop of Vercelli, who lived with his clergy as monks, refused at Milan to condemn Athanasius, and was exiled to Palestine and Egypt by Constantius. Also today: Peter Julian Eymard, apostle of the Eucharist, and Our Lady of the Angels (the Portiuncula).

The seller of purple at Philippi 'whose heart the Lord opened' to hear Paul by the river; she and her household were baptised, and she insisted the apostles lodge with her — the first Christian in Europe. Also today: Nicodemus, and the Finding of the relics of Stephen.

A farm boy who could barely learn Latin, sent to the village of Ars because 'there is not much love of God there', where for forty years he heard confessions up to sixteen hours a day, fought the devil at night, and drew a hundred thousand pilgrims a year. Patron of parish priests.

n: The Dedication of Saint Mary Major
b: The first church in the West dedicated to Mary, built by Pope Sixtus III after the Council of Ephesus (431). Legend tells of snow falling on the Esquiline in August to mark the site — 'Our Lady of the Snows'; white petals fall from the ceiling at Mass today. It houses the relics of the manger.

On the mountain Jesus' face shines like the sun, Moses and Elias speak with him, and the voice from the cloud says 'This is my beloved Son.' The Eastern Church's great August feast; the West adopted it in 1457 to mark the victory over the Turks at Belgrade. Hiroshima was bombed on this day in 1945.

Sixtus, seized while celebrating Mass in the catacomb of Callistus and beheaded in his chair under Valerian, four days before his deacon Lawrence; named in the Roman Canon. Cajetan (d. 1547), founder of the Theatines, who set up pawnshops that charged no interest for the poor of Naples.

t: Priest, founder of the Order of Preachers
b: A Castilian canon who sold his books to feed the starving, met the Albigensian heretics in Languedoc and saw that only poor, learned preachers could answer them, and founded the Dominicans — 'to praise, to bless, to preach'. Tradition gives him the Rosary. He spoke only to God or of God.

t: Virgin and martyr, patroness of Europe
b: Edith Stein, a Jewish philosopher, pupil of Husserl and atheist, who read Teresa of Ávila's autobiography in one night and said 'this is the truth'; baptised in 1922, a Carmelite in 1933, she was taken from her Dutch convent by the Gestapo and gassed at Auschwitz with her sister Rosa.

Archdeacon of Rome, ordered to hand over the Church's treasures, who presented the poor of the city: 'These are the treasures of the Church.' Roasted on a gridiron, he is said to have told his executioners, 'Turn me over, this side is done.' Rome's most loved martyr after Peter and Paul; the August meteors are his tears.

t: Virgin, foundress of the Poor Clares
b: A noble girl of eighteen who slipped out of her father's house on Palm Sunday night to have her hair cut by Francis at the Portiuncula, and for forty-two years at San Damiano fought popes to keep the 'privilege of poverty'. She drove the Saracens from Assisi's walls holding the Blessed Sacrament. Patroness of television.

A widow with four children who, under the direction of Francis de Sales, founded the Visitation nuns for women too frail for the great austerities; eighty-seven convents by her death. Her grandson was the father of Madame de Sévigné. Also today: Euplius, the deacon of Catania who carried the Gospels to his death.

Hippolytus, the learned priest who set himself up as the first antipope, and Pontian, the lawful pope, were deported together to the mines of Sardinia under Maximinus, reconciled there, and died. Hippolytus's Apostolic Tradition preserves the oldest Eucharistic Prayer still in use.

A Polish Franciscan who founded the City of the Immaculate, the largest friary in the world, and a mission in Nagasaki. At Auschwitz, when a prisoner with a family was chosen for the starvation bunker, he stepped forward: 'I am a Catholic priest; I wish to take his place.' He led the dying in hymns for two weeks and was killed by injection.

n: The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: At the end of her life Mary was taken body and soul into heaven — believed since the earliest centuries (the East calls it the Dormition), defined by Pius XII in 1950. 'A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet' (Rev 12). Harvests and herbs are blessed today across Europe.

The Magyar prince Vajk, baptised at ten, crowned with a crown sent by the pope in the year 1000, who made Hungary a Christian kingdom with ten bishoprics, laws against pagan practice, and open hands to the poor. His right hand is carried through Budapest on his feast. Also today: Roch, invoked against plague.

A canon of Kraków who received the habit from Dominic himself in Rome and preached from the Baltic to Kiev; fleeing the Tatars, he carried the Blessed Sacrament and a heavy statue of Mary across the Dnieper. 'The Apostle of the North.' Also today: Clare of Montefalco.

An innkeeper's daughter who became the mother of Constantine, and at nearly eighty went to Jerusalem, where she built the churches of the Nativity and the Ascension and, tradition says, found the True Cross. Also today: Agapitus of Palestrina, a boy martyr, and Alberto Hurtado of Chile.

A Norman missionary who preached a hundred parish missions, nursed plague victims in a barrel so as not to infect his community, founded the Eudists to train priests and the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity for penitent women, and first composed a Mass of the Sacred Heart (1672).

t: Abbot and Doctor of the Church
b: A Burgundian noble who entered Cîteaux at twenty-one with thirty relatives and friends, founded Clairvaux and sixty-eight daughter houses, ended a papal schism, preached the Second Crusade, fought Abelard, and wrote of the love of God with such sweetness that he is called the 'mellifluous doctor'. Dante makes him the guide to the Virgin.

Giuseppe Sarto, a village postman's son, who as pope lowered the age of First Communion to seven, urged daily Communion, reformed the Breviary and church music (Gregorian chant restored), codified canon law, and fought Modernism. He died a fortnight after the outbreak of the First World War, of grief, they said.

n: The Queenship of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: The octave of the Assumption: Mary crowned as queen beside her Son — 'the queen stood on thy right hand in gilded clothing' (Ps 44). Pius XII instituted the feast in 1954; the fifth Glorious Mystery of the Rosary is this scene.

Isabel Flores, a beauty of Lima who rubbed pepper on her face to spoil it, took the Dominican habit as a tertiary, lived in a hut in her parents' garden, and cared for the sick Indians and slaves of the city. She died at thirty-one. First saint of the Americas, patroness of Peru and the Philippines.

Usually identified with Nathanael, 'an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile', who asked whether anything good could come from Nazareth. Tradition sends him to Armenia, where he was flayed alive — Michelangelo painted his own face on the skin Bartholomew holds in the Last Judgement.

The saint-king who fed the poor at his own table, built the Sainte-Chapelle for the Crown of Thorns, judged under the oak of Vincennes, went twice on crusade and died of dysentery at Tunis. Also today: Joseph Calasanz, founder of the Piarists, the first free schools for the poor in Europe.

Pope for eighteen years during which the Roman Church argued over the Trinity; his deacon Callistus guided him. Also today: Teresa of Jesus Jornet, foundress of the Little Sisters of the Abandoned Aged, and Our Lady of Częstochowa, the Black Madonna of Poland.

A North African wife of a pagan with a violent temper, who wept and prayed for seventeen years for her brilliant, wayward son, followed him to Rome and Milan, and saw him baptised by Ambrose. She died at Ostia on the way home, after the shared vision Augustine describes in the Confessions: 'Bury my body anywhere; only remember me at the altar.'

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: The rhetorician of Thagaste who kept a mistress, joined the Manichees, heard Ambrose, and in a Milan garden heard a child sing 'take up and read'; then bishop of Hippo for thirty-five years, author of the Confessions and the City of God, the most influential Christian thinker after Paul. 'Our heart is restless until it rests in thee.'

n: The Passion of Saint John the Baptist
b: Herod Antipas, bound by an oath to a dancing girl, had the Baptist beheaded in the fortress of Machaerus and the head brought in on a dish. 'He must increase, but I must decrease' — the forerunner goes before Christ in death as in birth.

n: Margaret Ward, Anne Line and Margaret Clitherow
b: Margaret Ward, hanged at Tyburn for smuggling a rope to a priest in the Bridewell; Anne Line, hanged in 1601 for harbouring priests; Margaret Clitherow, the butcher's wife of York pressed to death under a door. The three women among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales. Also today: Felix and Adauctus.

An Irish monk of Iona sent to King Oswald, who translated his sermons himself; he walked everywhere, gave away the king's horse to a beggar, ransomed slaves and made them priests, and founded Lindisfarne. Bede loved him above all the saints of the North. Also today: Raymond Nonnatus, ransomer of captives.

A Greek hermit of the Rhône delta whose hind, wounded by the king's hunting arrow, fled to his cave; he founded the abbey of Saint-Gilles, a great stop on the road to Compostela. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, patron of cripples and beggars; a hundred and sixty English churches bear his name.

A hundred and ninety-one bishops, priests and religious murdered in the Paris prisons of the Carmes, Saint-Firmin and the Abbaye on 2–3 September 1792 for refusing the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Also today: Stephen of Hungary (traditional date) and William of Roskilde.

t: Pope and Doctor of the Church
b: Prefect of Rome who sold his estates for monasteries, was dragged from his cloister to be pope in a plague year, fed the city, faced the Lombards, sent Augustine to England, wrote the Pastoral Rule for every bishop since, and called himself 'servant of the servants of God'. The chant bears his name.

A Norman noblewoman who lived as a hermit in a cave on Monte Pellegrino; when her bones were found in 1624 and carried through Palermo, the plague ceased. Also today: Moses the Lawgiver in the Roman Martyrology, and Rose of Viterbo.

t: Virgin, foundress of the Missionaries of Charity
b: Anjezë Bojaxhiu of Skopje, a Loreto nun teaching in Calcutta who on a train to Darjeeling heard 'the call within the call' to serve the poorest of the poor; she picked the dying off the streets, and her sisters now work in a hundred and thirty countries. Nobel Peace Prize 1979. Her diaries revealed fifty years of spiritual darkness borne in faith.

An Irish princess who fled a Viking marriage across the sea to Cumbria and founded St Bees; oaths were sworn on her bracelet for centuries. Also today: Zachary the prophet, father of the Baptist, in the Martyrology, and Eleutherius, abbot of Spoleto.

Grandson of Clovis, whose two brothers were murdered by their uncles; he cut off his own royal hair and became a hermit, then a priest, founding the monastery at Saint-Cloud near Paris. Also today: Regina of Autun, virgin martyr, and Melchior Grodziecki and Stephen Pongracz, Jesuit martyrs of Košice.

n: The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: Nine months after the Immaculate Conception, the Church keeps Mary's birthday — one of only three birthdays in the calendar, with Christ's and the Baptist's. Kept since the sixth century in Jerusalem, at the church built where the house of Joachim and Anne was believed to stand.

A Catalan Jesuit who for forty years met every slave ship arriving at Cartagena, boarding with food, medicine and interpreters, baptising three hundred thousand and calling himself 'the slave of the slaves for ever'. He spent his last four years paralysed and neglected in his room.

An Augustinian friar of the Marches who preached daily for thirty years, visited the slums and prisons, and had a devotion to the souls in purgatory; the bread blessed in his name is given to the sick. Also today: Ambrose Barlow, Benedictine martyr of Lancashire.

Two brothers, servants of Eugenia, beheaded under Valerian; the tomb of Hyacinth was found untouched in the catacomb of Bassilla in 1845, the bones charred, with his name intact. Also today: Paphnutius the bishop, who bore the marks of Diocletian's persecution to the Council of Nicaea.

n: The Most Holy Name of Mary
b: Extended to the whole Church by Innocent XI after the relief of Vienna from the Turks on 12 September 1683 by John Sobieski, who had commended his army to Mary. Also today: Guy of Anderlecht, the poor man's saint of Brussels.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: 'Golden-mouthed', the greatest preacher of the Greek Church, a hermit turned priest of Antioch, dragged to Constantinople as patriarch, where he sold the palace plate for the poor, denounced the empress's vanity, and was exiled twice, dying on a forced march in Pontus: 'Glory be to God for all things.' The Byzantine liturgy bears his name.

n: The Exaltation of the Holy Cross
b: The dedication of Constantine's church of the Holy Sepulchre in 335, when the Cross found by Helena was lifted up for the people to see; and the recovery of the relic from the Persians by Heraclius in 629. 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up.'

The day after the Cross: Mary standing beneath it, 'and thy own soul a sword shall pierce.' The Seven Sorrows — Simeon's prophecy, the flight into Egypt, the loss in the Temple, the way of the cross, the crucifixion, the deposition, the burial — are the Servites' devotion; the Stabat Mater is the day's hymn.

Cornelius, the pope who readmitted the lapsed after penance against the rigorist Novatian, exiled and killed in 253; Cyprian, the rich rhetorician-bishop of Carthage who supported him, wrote On the Unity of the Church, and was beheaded in 258 after a trial whose record survives: 'Thanks be to God.' Both are named in the Roman Canon.

Bellarmine, the Jesuit cardinal of the Counter-Reformation controversies and Galileo's judge, who gave his money to the poor and slept on a straw mattress. Hildegard (d. 1179), the Rhineland abbess whose visions, music, medicine and letters to emperors made her the most remarkable woman of her century; Doctor of the Church since 2012.

A dull, absent-minded boy who was refused by the Capuchins and made a stable hand by the Conventuals, ordained by a lucky examination, and then spent thirty-five years being hidden by his superiors because he rose into the air at Mass, at the name of Mary, at the sight of a lamb. Patron of pilots and of examinees.

Bishop of Benevento beheaded at Pozzuoli under Diocletian. In Naples cathedral a vial of his dried blood liquefies three times a year, usually today, before a crowd that watches for the omen; the years it fails have brought Vesuvius, cholera and war. Also today: Theodore of Canterbury.

n: Andrew Kim Tae-gŏn, Paul Chŏng Ha-sang and Companions
b: A hundred and three martyrs of a Church that Koreans founded themselves from books, without a missionary, in 1784. Andrew Kim, the first Korean priest, beheaded at twenty-five on the Han river; Paul Chŏng, a lay catechist; and women, children and old men, killed in the persecutions of 1839, 1846 and 1866.

Levi the tax collector, called from his customs booth at Capharnaum — 'and he rose up, and followed him' — who gave a dinner for Jesus and his fellow publicans. The first Gospel bears his name, written for Jews to show Jesus as the Messiah of the prophets. Tradition sends him to Ethiopia.

An Egyptian legion of Christians in the Roman army who refused to sacrifice — or, in another telling, to slaughter innocent Christians — at Agaunum in the Alps and were decimated twice and then massacred. The abbey of Saint-Maurice has kept the office in their memory without interruption since 515.

A Capuchin of the Gargano who bore the stigmata for fifty years, heard confessions for hours a day and read hearts, built the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza hospital, and was suspended for years by a suspicious Vatican. His Mass at San Giovanni Rotondo drew millions. Also today: Linus, second pope.

The feast of the Mercedarians, founded in 1218 by Peter Nolasco to ransom Christian captives from the Moors, its members vowing to take a captive's place if needed. Also today: Gerard of Csanád, the Venetian bishop martyred by pagan Magyars — Budapest's Gellért hill is his.

A hermit of the forests north of Moscow who founded the Trinity Lavra, the mother house of Russian monasticism, and blessed Prince Dmitri before the battle of Kulikovo that broke the Tatar yoke. Russia's most loved saint. Also today: Finbarr of Cork, and Cleophas of Emmaus in the Martyrology.

Twin brothers, physicians of Cilicia who took no fees — the 'unmercenary healers' — beheaded under Diocletian. Justinian rebuilt their church; the Medici took them as patrons; they are named in the Roman Canon. Patrons of doctors, surgeons and pharmacists.

A Gascon peasant's son, tutor in the house of the general of the galleys, who found God among the galley slaves and the country poor, founded the Congregation of the Mission, the Ladies of Charity and, with Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity, and organised the relief of Lorraine in the Thirty Years' War. Patron of all charitable works.

'Good King Wenceslas', duke of Bohemia, raised by his grandmother Ludmila, who built churches and gave to the poor, and was murdered at the church door by his brother Boleslav. Lawrence Ruiz (d. 1637), a Filipino clerk and father of three, tortured to death at Nagasaki: 'Had I a thousand lives, I would offer them all.'

The three angels named in Scripture: Michael, 'who is like God?', captain of the heavenly host against the dragon; Gabriel, who announced the Baptist and the Christ; Raphael, 'God heals', the companion of Tobias. Michaelmas, once a quarter day of the English year.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: The scholar of Stridon who learned Hebrew from a rabbi, dreamed that Christ called him a Ciceronian rather than a Christian, served Pope Damasus, and in a cave at Bethlehem translated the whole Bible into the Latin of this app — the Vulgate, the Bible of the West for a thousand years. Irascible, brilliant, penitent; painted with a lion and a skull. 'Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.'
